d: A crypto token built around a joke, an animal, a person or an internet trend. It usually has no product or income behind it, so its price moves only on attention and buying and selling.
The unique address of a token on its blockchain. Names and tickers can be copied by anyone — the contract address cannot, so always check it before buying.

A DEX (decentralized exchange, like Raydium or PancakeSwap) lets you swap tokens straight from your own wallet. A CEX (centralized exchange, like Binance) holds your money for you and lists only tokens it has checked.
The money sitting in a token's trading pool. With little liquidity, even a small sale moves the price a lot and you may not be able to sell at a fair price.
Locking or burning the pool's liquidity means the creator cannot pull it out. Unlocked liquidity is the classic way rug pulls happen.
When the creators or insiders suddenly pull out the pool's money or dump their coins, so the price falls to almost zero and buyers cannot get out.
A scam token you can buy but cannot sell, because the contract blocks or heavily taxes sales. Always check that other holders have actually sold.
On launchpads such as pump.fun, a new token is first sold on a price curve: every purchase pushes the price up. When enough money comes in, the token «graduates».
The moment a launchpad token fills its bonding curve and moves to a real DEX pool. Only a few percent of new tokens ever get there.
A bot or trader that buys a token in the very first seconds after launch, often to sell to later buyers at a higher price.
A creator who buys a large share of their own token from many wallets at launch to look like many different holders. A warning sign of a planned dump.
The wallet of the token's creator. If it holds a big share of the supply, the creator can crash the price at any time by selling.
The share of all coins held by the 10 biggest wallets. The higher it is (for example over 30%), the easier it is for a few people to crash the price.
«Key opinion leader» — an influencer with a big audience. KOLs are often paid to promote tokens, sometimes after buying them cheap themselves.
A group pushes the price up with hype and buying, then sells to the newcomers at the top. Latecomers are left holding the losses.
The difference between the price you see and the price you actually get. In thin memecoin pools it can be 5–20% or more on a single trade.
Market cap is price × coins in circulation. FDV (fully diluted value) is price × all coins that will ever exist. A big gap means many coins can still be unlocked and sold.
«Do your own research». A reminder that nobody — not an influencer, not a website — is responsible for your money but you.
Buying a token quickly on hype without checking it. The fastest way to lose money on memecoins.
Slang for people who sell at the first drop (paper hands) or hold through any crash (diamond hands). Neither is a strategy by itself.
